{{Short description|Theorem about convergence of Fourier series}}'''Wiener–Lévy theorem''' is a theorem in [[Fourier analysis]], which states that a function of an [[Absolute convergence|absolutely convergent]] [[Fourier series]] has an absolutely convergent Fourier series under some conditions. The theorem was named after [[Norbert Wiener]] and [[Paul Lévy (mathematician)|Paul Lévy]].

[[Norbert Wiener]] first proved Wiener's 1/''f'' theorem,<ref>{{cite journal |last=Wiener |first=N. |year=1932 |title=Tauberian Theorems |journal=[[Annals of Mathematics]] |volume=33 |issue=1 |pages=1–100 |jstor=1968102 |doi=10.2307/1968102}}</ref> see [[Wiener's 1/f theorem|Wiener's theorem]]. It states that if {{math|''f''}} has absolutely convergent Fourier series and is never zero, then its inverse {{math|1/''f''}} also has an absolutely convergent Fourier series.

==Wiener–Levy theorem==

[[Paul Lévy (mathematician)|Paul Levy]] generalized Wiener's result,<ref>{{cite journal |last=Lévy |first=P. |year=1935 |title=Sur la convergence absolue des séries de Fourier |journal=[[Compositio Mathematica]] |volume=1 |pages=1–14 }}</ref> showing that

Let <math> F(\theta ) = \sum\limits_{k = -\infty}^\infty c_k e^{ik\theta}, \quad\theta  \in [0,2\pi ]</math> be an absolutely convergent Fourier series with

: <math>\|F\| = \sum\limits_{k = -\infty}^\infty |c_k| < \infty. </math>

The values of <math>F(\theta )</math> lie on a curve <math>C</math>, and <math>H(t)</math> is an analytic (not necessarily single-valued) function of a complex variable which is regular at every point of <math>C</math>. Then <math>H[F(\theta )]</math> has an absolutely convergent Fourier series.

The proof can be found in the Zygmund's classic book ''[[Trigonometric Series]]''.<ref>{{cite book |last=Zygmund |first=A. |author-link=Antoni Zygmund |year=2002 |title=Trigonometric Series|title-link=Trigonometric Series |publisher=Cambridge University Press |location=Cambridge |page=245 }}</ref>

==Example==
Let <math>H(\theta )=\ln(\theta )</math> and <math>F(\theta ) = \sum\limits_{k = 0}^\infty  p_k e^{ik\theta},(\sum\limits_{k = 0}^\infty p_k = 1 </math>) is [[Characteristic function (probability theory)|characteristic function]] of discrete [[probability distribution]].  So <math>F(\theta ) </math> is an absolutely convergent Fourier series. If <math>F(\theta )</math> has no zeros, then we have
:<math>H[F(\theta )] = \ln \left( \sum\limits_{k = 0}^\infty  p_k e^{ik\theta} \right) = \sum_{k = 0}^\infty c_k e^{ik\theta},  </math>
where <math>\|H\| = \sum\limits_{k = 0}^\infty |c_k| < \infty. </math>

The statistical application of this example can be found in discrete pseudo [[compound Poisson distribution]]<ref name=zhang>{{Cite journal |first =Zhang  | last = Huiming |last2=Li |first2=Bo |author3=G. Jay Kerns |title=A characterization of signed discrete infinitely divisible distributions|journal=Studia Scientiarum Mathematicarum Hungarica|volume=54  |year=2017|pages=446–470|url=https://akademiai.com/doi/abs/10.1556/012.2017.54.4.1377 |doi=10.1556/012.2017.54.4.1377|arxiv=1701.03892}}</ref> and [[zero-inflated model]].

 If a discrete r.v. <math>X</math> with <math>\Pr(X = i) = P_{i}</math>, <math>i \in \mathbb N</math>, has the probability generating function of the form

:<math> P(z) = \sum\limits_{i = 0}^\infty  P_{i} z^{i} = \exp \left\{\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{\infty} \alpha_{i} \lambda (z^{i} - 1) \right\},z=e^{ik\theta}</math>

where <math>\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{\infty} \alpha_{i} = 1</math>, <math>\sum \limits_{i =
    1}^{\infty} \left| \alpha_{i} \right| < \infty</math>, <math>\alpha_{i} \in
  \mathbb{R}</math>, and <math>\lambda > 0</math>. Then <math>X</math> is said to have the discrete pseudo compound Poisson distribution, abbreviated DPCP.

We denote it as <math>X \sim DPCP({\alpha _1}\lambda,{\alpha _2}\lambda, \cdots )</math>.
